pos: n. (Pierre du Moulin, 1568–1658, pastor at Charenton, professor at Sedan, and champion of Dort against Arminius and Amyraut)
etymology: Greek Petros, a rock; French du Moulin, of the mill.
biblical_def: Pierre du Moulin survived the St Bartholomew's Day Massacre as a child, studied at Cambridge and Leiden, and taught philosophy at Leiden, where Hugo Grotius was among his pupils. From 1599 to 1620 he was pastor of the Reformed church of Paris at Charenton and the most formidable Protestant controversialist in France, writing against the Jesuits, against the papal claims, and against the doctrine of the mass; his Buckler of the Faith of 1618 answered the king's Jesuit confessor point by point. He was equally firm against the Remonstrants. His Anatomy of Arminianism (1619) was one of the most widely read Reformed treatments of the controversy decided at Dort, and he led the French national synod of Alais in 1620 to adopt the Canons of Dort. Driven from Paris by royal displeasure in 1620, he spent the rest of his long life as professor of theology at the Protestant academy of Sedan, and from there he attacked Amyraut's hypothetical universalism as a revival of Arminianism under Reformed terms. James I of England valued him and gave him a prebend at Canterbury. His theology was that of Dort, resting on the sovereignty of grace: “by grace are ye saved through faith; and that not of yourselves: it is the gift of God” (Eph 2:8).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a controversialist as one who carries on a controversy, and Arminianism as the doctrines of the Arminians.
webster_full: CONTROVER'SIALIST, n. One who carries on a controversy; a disputant.
ARMIN'IANISM, n. The peculiar doctrines or tenets of the Arminians.
BUCK'LER, n. A kind of shield, or piece of defensive armor.
scriptures: Eph 2:8
For by grace are ye saved through faith; and that not of yourselves: it is the gift of God:
Rom 9:16
So then it is not of him that willeth, nor of him that runneth, but of God that sheweth mercy.
Jude 1:3

Beloved, when I gave all diligence to write unto you of the common salvation, it was needful for me to write unto you, and exhort you that ye should earnestly contend for the faith which was once delivered unto the saints.
But sanctify the Lord God in your hearts: and be ready always to give an answer to every man that asketh you a reason of the hope that is in you with meekness and fear:
corruption_summary: The French champion of Dort who answered Rome, Arminius, and Amyraut in turn.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. Du Moulin's career shows why the Reformed churches of France adopted Dort: they had learned that a doctrine of grace that leaves the decisive act to the human will is a doctrine Rome can accept. His answer to the Remonstrants was Paul's, “it is not of him that willeth, nor of him that runneth, but of God that sheweth mercy” (Rom 9:16).

The principle to recover is the readiness he showed on every front, “to give an answer to every man that asketh you a reason of the hope that is in you” (1Pe 3:15). The French church that later gave Amyraut a hearing and silence instead of an answer did not find the peace it sought.
usage: “it is the gift of God” (Eph 2:8) — the Anatomy of Arminianism in brief.
“not of him that willeth” (Rom 9:16) — his answer to the Remonstrants.
“earnestly contend for the faith” (Jude 1:3) — sixty years of controversy.

pos: n. (Jean Daillé, 1594–1670, pastor at Charenton and author of On the Right Use of the Fathers, 1632)
etymology: French Jean, from Hebrew Yochanan; Daillé, a family name.
biblical_def: Jean Daillé was tutor to the grandsons of the Huguenot statesman Philippe du Plessis-Mornay, travelled with them through Italy and England, and from 1626 until his death was one of the pastors of the Reformed church of Paris at Charenton, the most distinguished pulpit in French Protestantism. His fame rests on a single book, the Treatise on the Right Use of the Fathers of 1632, translated into English in 1651 and read across Protestant Europe. Rome's apologists argued that the fathers of the first centuries were the authoritative interpreters of Scripture and that their consent proved the Roman doctrine. Daillé answered that the fathers cannot serve as judges of controversies: many of their writings are lost, many surviving works are spurious or interpolated, their language is often obscure, they wrote on questions other than ours, they frequently contradicted one another and sometimes themselves, and they never claimed for their own words the authority Rome claimed for them. The fathers are witnesses to be honoured and read, but Scripture alone is the judge. Daillé also preached long series of expository sermons, on Philippians and Colossians among others, and in the Saumur controversy sided with Amyraut. His rule was the prophet's: “To the law and to the testimony: if they speak not according to this word, it is because there is no light in them” (Isa 8:20).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a father in theology as one of the early teachers of the church, and tradition as that which is handed down without writing.
webster_full: FA'THER, n. The appellation of the first Christian writers, as Augustine, Jerome, and others, who wrote in the early ages of the church.

TRADI'TION, n. Any thing transmitted orally from father to son, or from ancestors to posterity; that body of doctrine and discipline, supposed to have been put forth by Christ or his apostles, and not committed to writing.
SPU'RIOUS, a. Not genuine; not proceeding from the true source, or from the source pretended.
scriptures: Isa 8:20
To the law and to the testimony: if they speak not according to this word, it is because there is no light in them.
Joh 5:39
Search the scriptures; for in them ye think ye have eternal life: and they are they which testify of me.
All scripture is given by inspiration of God, and is profitable for doctrine, for reproof, for correction, for instruction in righteousness:
Gal 1:8
But though we, or an angel from heaven, preach any other gospel unto you than that which we have preached unto you, let him be accursed.
corruption_summary: The pastor who showed that the fathers are witnesses, not judges.
corruption_paragraphs: The dictionary names the claim that patristic consent is a rule of faith beside Scripture as a corruption of sola Scriptura. Daillé's demonstration that the fathers disagree, that their texts are uncertain, and that they did not write to settle our questions shows that an appeal to them as judges is an appeal to an authority that cannot speak with one voice. Christ sent His hearers elsewhere: “Search the scriptures” (Joh 5:39), for “they are they which testify of me” (Joh 5:39).

The modern form of the error is the recovery of the fathers as a rule of interpretation by evangelicals weary of Protestant division, which often ends in Rome or Constantinople. The principle to recover is Daillé's balance: read the fathers with gratitude, test them by Scripture, and let no voice, however ancient, preach “any other gospel unto you than that which we have preached unto you” (Gal 1:8).
roots_summary: Hebrew torah (H8451), law; teudah (H8584), testimony; Greek ereunao (G2045), to search.
usage: “To the law and to the testimony” (Isa 8:20) — the judge of controversies.
“All scripture is given by inspiration of God” (2Ti 3:16) — what no father claimed for himself.
“preach any other gospel unto you” (Gal 1:8) — the limit on every authority.

pos: n. (Pierre Jurieu, 1637–1713, Huguenot theologian at Sedan and Rotterdam, adversary of Bossuet, and interpreter of prophecy)
etymology: Greek Petros, a rock; French Jurieu, a family name.
biblical_def: Pierre Jurieu was a grandson of Pierre du Moulin, trained at Saumur and Sedan, and professor of theology and Hebrew at Sedan until the academy was suppressed by Louis XIV in 1681. He then became professor at the École Illustre and pastor of the Walloon church in Rotterdam, where he spent the rest of his life as the most combative voice of the Huguenot dispersion. He answered Bossuet's attacks on Protestantism; wrote against Claude Pajon's doctrine of conversion as a betrayal of efficacious grace; quarrelled with his colleague Pierre Bayle over toleration; and from 1686 to 1689 published Pastoral Letters smuggled into France to strengthen the persecuted Protestants of the Desert, in which he argued that a king who breaks the fundamental laws of his realm may be resisted. In 1686 he published The Accomplishment of the Prophecies, a historicist reading of Revelation that identified the papacy as the beast and predicted the fall of Antichrist and the restoration of the French churches within a few years; when the date passed unfulfilled, his reputation suffered. He also encouraged the early inspirés of the Cévennes. He read his age through Paul's prophecy that a falling away would come first, and “that man of sin be revealed, the son of perdition” (2Th 2:3).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines prophecy as a foretelling, and Antichrist as a great adversary of Christ.
webster_full: PROPH'ECY, n. A foretelling; prediction; a declaration of something to come.
AN'TICHRIST, n. A great adversary of Christ; the man of sin; described 2 Thess. ii.
DIS'PERSION, n. The act of scattering; the state of being scattered.
scriptures: Let no man deceive you by any means: for that day shall not come, except there come a falling away first, and that man of sin be revealed, the son of perdition;
Rev 13:7
And it was given unto him to make war with the saints, and to overcome them: and power was given him over all kindreds, and tongues, and nations.
Rev 17:5
And upon her forehead was a name written, MYSTERY, BABYLON THE GREAT, THE MOTHER OF HARLOTS AND ABOMINATIONS OF THE EARTH.
Dan 7:25

And he shall speak great words against the most High, and shall wear out the saints of the most High, and think to change times and laws: and they shall be given into his hand until a time and times and the dividing of time.
corruption_summary: A Huguenot polemicist of the dispersion who read the papacy as Antichrist and set dates for its fall.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. Jurieu's identification of the papacy with the man of sin stood in the line of the Reformers and the Westminster divines, and his defence of efficacious grace against Pajon was sound. The beast of Revelation that was given power “to make war with the saints, and to overcome them” (Rev 13:7) looked to the persecuted of the Desert like the power that sent them to the galleys.

His error was the date. Christ said the day and hour are known to no man, and an interpreter who names the year of Antichrist's fall stakes the credibility of prophecy on his arithmetic. His encouragement of the inspirés was a second error, as their ruin showed. The principle to recover is that the prophecies of Daniel and Revelation comfort the church by their certainty, not by our calendars.
roots_lines: Greek apostasia (G646) — a falling away, apostasy; 2 Thessalonians 2:3.
usage: “that man of sin be revealed, the son of perdition” (2Th 2:3) — his reading of the papacy.
“to make war with the saints” (Rev 13:7) — the Desert under Louis XIV.
“shall wear out the saints of the most High” (Dan 7:25) — the persecutions he chronicled.

pos: n. (Jean Claude, 1619–1687, pastor at Charenton, defender of the Reformed doctrine of the Supper against Arnauld and Bossuet, expelled from France in 1685)
biblical_def: Jean Claude was pastor at Nîmes and Montauban before he was called in 1666 to Charenton, where he became the leading minister of French Protestantism in its last decades of legal existence. He is remembered for his controversy with the Jansenist theologians Antoine Arnauld and Pierre Nicole, whose massive Perpetuity of the Faith concerning the Eucharist argued that the church had always believed in transubstantiation and that the Protestant doctrine was a novelty. Claude answered them in a series of works showing from the fathers and from history that the doctrine of a corporeal change of the elements arose in the Middle Ages, and that Christ's sacrifice is once for all. In 1678 he held a private conference with Bossuet on the authority of the church. When the Edict of Nantes was revoked in October 1685, the king made an exception to the rule that pastors had fifteen days to leave: Claude was ordered out of the kingdom within twenty-four hours, escorted to the frontier by a royal footman. He settled at The Hague, where he wrote The Complaint of the Protestants, an account of the persecution that the French government had burned. The doctrine he defended is Hebrews': Christ, “after he had offered one sacrifice for sins for ever, sat down on the right hand of God” (Heb 10:12).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines transubstantiation as the supposed change of the bread and wine into the body and blood of Christ.
webster_full: TRANSUBSTANTIA'TION, n. In the Romish theology, the supposed conversion of the bread and wine in the eucharist into the body and blood of Christ.
EU'CHARIST, n. The sacrament of the Lord's supper.
BAN'ISHMENT, n. The act of a prince or government, compelling a citizen to leave his country.
scriptures: But this man, after he had offered one sacrifice for sins for ever, sat down on the right hand of God;
And he took bread, and gave thanks, and brake it, and gave unto them, saying, This is my body which is given for you: this do in remembrance of me.
For as often as ye eat this bread, and drink this cup, ye do shew the Lord's death till he come.
Heb 9:28
So Christ was once offered to bear the sins of many; and unto them that look for him shall he appear the second time without sin unto salvation.
corruption_summary: The Charenton pastor who proved transubstantiation a medieval novelty and was expelled in a day.
corruption_paragraphs: The dictionary names transubstantiation as a corruption of the Lord's Supper, as Claude did. Christ instituted a memorial, “this do in remembrance of me” (Luk 22:19), and the apostle says the Supper shows “the Lord's death till he come” (1Co 11:26): a death past and a coming future, with the Lord bodily in heaven between. A doctrine that makes the bread His body and the mass His sacrifice contradicts the once-for-all offering of Hebrews.

The argument from perpetuity, that the church has always believed it, is answered by history, and Claude's work remains a model of the Protestant use of the fathers as witnesses. The principle to recover is that “Christ was once offered to bear the sins of many” (Heb 9:28), and that no priest can offer Him again.
usage: “offered one sacrifice for sins for ever” (Heb 10:12) — against the mass.
“this do in remembrance of me” (Luk 22:19) — the Supper as memorial.
“Christ was once offered” (Heb 9:28) — the end of the argument from perpetuity.

pos: n. (the armed return of the exiled Waldenses from Switzerland to their Alpine valleys in August 1689, under Henri Arnaud)
etymology: French Glorieuse Rentrée, the glorious re-entry, the Waldenses' own name for it.
biblical_def: The Glorious Return was the march by which the Waldenses recovered their homeland. In January 1686, under pressure from Louis XIV, Duke Victor Amadeus II of Savoy ordered the Protestants of the Piedmont valleys to abandon their faith or leave. Those who resisted were overwhelmed; some two thousand were killed, more than eight thousand imprisoned in the duke's fortresses, where many died, and in 1687 the survivors, perhaps three thousand, were released into exile in Switzerland. On the night of 16–17 August 1689, some nine hundred of the exiles, led by their pastor Henri Arnaud, crossed Lake Geneva in boats from Prangins and marched for twelve days over the high Alpine passes, fighting their way through Savoyard and French troops, until they reached the valleys of Piedmont. Through the winter they held the rock fortress of the Balsiglia above the Germanasca valley against an army many times their number; in May 1690, when the French brought cannon and the last assault was expected, the defenders escaped through the fog by night. Weeks later Victor Amadeus broke with France and joined the Grand Alliance, made peace with the Waldenses, and allowed the exiles to come home. They had prayed with Israel in exile, “If I forget thee, O Jerusalem, let my right hand forget her cunning” (Psa 137:5).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines exile as banishment, the state of being expelled from one's country, and return as the act of coming back.
webster_full: EX'ILE, n. Banishment; the state of being expelled from one's native country or place of residence.
RETURN', n. The act of returning or coming back to the same place or condition.
FOR'TRESS, n. Any fortified place; a fort; a castle; a stronghold.
scriptures: If I forget thee, O Jerusalem, let my right hand forget her cunning.
And the ransomed of the LORD shall return, and come to Zion with songs and everlasting joy upon their heads: they shall obtain joy and gladness, and sorrow and sighing shall flee away.
And there is hope in thine end, saith the LORD, that thy children shall come again to their own border.
If it had not been the LORD who was on our side, when men rose up against us:
corruption_summary: Nine hundred Waldensian exiles who marched home over the Alps and held their valleys.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The Glorious Return is a story of providence before it is a story of arms. A small company of exiles with no hope of victory held out until a political reversal no one foresaw opened the way home, and the Waldenses themselves read it so: “If it had not been the LORD who was on our side, when men rose up against us” (Psa 124:2).

The principle to recover is the hope of the prophets for a scattered people: “there is hope in thine end, saith the LORD, that thy children shall come again to their own border” (Jer 31:17). The church's earthly homes are given and taken by God, and the Return foreshadows the greater return of Isa 35:10, when “the ransomed of the LORD shall return, and come to Zion with songs” (Isa 35:10).
roots_summary: Hebrew shakach (H7911), to forget; shub (H7725), to return; padah (H6299), to ransom.
roots_lines: Hebrew shub (H7725) — to turn back, return; Isaiah 35:10.
usage: “If I forget thee, O Jerusalem” (Psa 137:5) — the exiles in Switzerland.
“thy children shall come again to their own border” (Jer 31:17) — August 1689.
“If it had not been the LORD who was on our side” (Psa 124:2) — the Balsiglia.

pos: n. (Henri Arnaud, 1641–1721, Waldensian pastor who led the Glorious Return of 1689 and later the Waldensian colony in Württemberg)
etymology: Germanic Heimrich, home ruler; French Arnaud, from Germanic arn, eagle, and wald, rule.
biblical_def: Henri Arnaud was born in the Dauphiné, raised in the Waldensian valleys of Piedmont, and educated at Basel and Geneva. He served as pastor in the valleys and shared the catastrophe of 1686, when the duke of Savoy's edict and the French and Savoyard troops destroyed the Waldensian communities and drove the survivors into exile. In Switzerland he became the chief organizer of the plan to return. He made contact with William of Orange, who was preparing to take the English throne and was forming a coalition against Louis XIV, and secured encouragement and money. In August 1689 he led some nine hundred armed exiles across Lake Geneva and over the Alps, combining the offices of pastor and commander: he preached to his men, led their prayers, and directed their march and their defence of the Balsiglia through the winter of 1689–90. When peace came he served again as pastor in the valleys. In 1698, when the duke expelled Waldenses born in French territory, Arnaud led some three thousand of them into exile once more, to Württemberg in Germany, where he ministered at Schönenberg until his death. His history of the Return was published in 1710. He told his men what Nehemiah told the builders: “remember the Lord, which is great and terrible, and fight for your brethren” (Neh 4:14).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a chaplain as a clergyman who performs divine service in an army, and a colony as a body of people transplanted to a remote country.
webster_full: CHAP'LAIN, n. A clergyman who is appointed to perform divine service in the army or navy, or in a public institution.
COL'ONY, n. A company or body of people transplanted from their mother country to a remote province or country to cultivate and inhabit it.
COMMAND'ER, n. A leader; the chief officer of an army, or of any division of it.
scriptures: Neh 4:14

And I looked, and rose up, and said unto the nobles, and to the rulers, and to the rest of the people, Be not ye afraid of them: remember the Lord, which is great and terrible, and fight for your brethren, your sons, and your daughters, your wives, and your houses.
Jos 1:9
Have not I commanded thee? Be strong and of a good courage; be not afraid, neither be thou dismayed: for the LORD thy God is with thee whithersoever thou goest.
And he led them forth by the right way, that they might go to a city of habitation.
The eternal God is thy refuge, and underneath are the everlasting arms: and he shall thrust out the enemy from before thee; and shall say, Destroy them.
corruption_summary: A pastor who led his exiled people home over the Alps, and then into exile again.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. Arnaud's double office raises the question the Huguenots and Covenanters also faced: whether a minister may bear arms. The Return was a defence of a people driven from their homes by a sovereign who had broken his own predecessors' concessions, under the protection of a Protestant prince, and Arnaud's leadership was that of a pastor with his flock in extremity, not of a cleric seeking power.

The principle to recover is the steadiness of faith across reversals. Arnaud led his people home and then, nine years later, out again, and in both journeys the confession was Moses': “The eternal God is thy refuge, and underneath are the everlasting arms” (Deu 33:27). The Lord who “led them forth by the right way, that they might go to a city of habitation” (Psa 107:7) does not always lead by the road His people would choose.
roots_summary: Hebrew yare (H3372), to fear; chazaq (H2388), to be strong; meonah (H4585), refuge, dwelling.
roots_lines: Hebrew chazaq (H2388) — to be strong, take courage; Joshua 1:9.
usage: “remember the Lord, which is great and terrible” (Neh 4:14) — the pastor-commander's charge.
“Be strong and of a good courage” (Jos 1:9) — the crossing of the Alps.
“underneath are the everlasting arms” (Deu 33:27) — Württemberg, 1698.

pos: n. (Josué Janavel, 1617–1690, Waldensian peasant captain of Rorà who resisted the massacre of 1655)
etymology: Hebrew Yehoshua, the LORD saves, through French Josué; Janavel, a family name of the valleys.
biblical_def: Josué Janavel was a farmer of Rorà in the Luserna valley of Piedmont. In April 1655 the Marquis of Pianezza quartered an army of Savoyard, French, and Irish troops on the Waldensian villages and, after they had been received into the people's homes, turned them loose in the massacre remembered as the Piedmont Easter, in which some seventeen hundred Waldenses were killed, many with great cruelty. At Rorà, Janavel gathered a handful of men, at first only six or seven, and ambushed the columns sent up the mountain to destroy the village, driving them back again and again. When the marquis captured his wife and three daughters and threatened to burn them unless he surrendered and renounced his faith, Janavel answered that he would rather they died than that he deny Christ, and commended them to God. His resistance, with that of others in the valleys, helped bring the duke to the Treaty of Pinerolo in August 1655. Janavel was later exiled to Geneva. In 1689, too old to march, he wrote the military instructions that guided Henri Arnaud on the Glorious Return, and he died the next year. His victories were Gideon's lesson: “The people that are with thee are too many for me” (Jud 7:2), and Jehoshaphat's: “the battle is not yours, but God's” (2Ch 20:15).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a captain as the commander of a company, and an ambuscade as a lying in wait to attack by surprise.
webster_full: CAP'TAIN, n. A head or chief officer; the commander of a troop of horse, a company of infantry, or a ship.
AMBUSCA'DE, n. A private station in which troops lie concealed with a view to attack their enemy by surprise.
MAS'SACRE, n. The slaughter of numbers of human beings, with circumstances of cruelty.
scriptures: Jud 7:2
And the LORD said unto Gideon, The people that are with thee are too many for me to give the Midianites into their hands, lest Israel vaunt themselves against me, saying, Mine own hand hath saved me.

And he said, Hearken ye, all Judah, and ye inhabitants of Jerusalem, and thou king Jehoshaphat, Thus saith the LORD unto you, Be not afraid nor dismayed by reason of this great multitude; for the battle is not yours, but God's.
Psa 79:3
Their blood have they shed like water round about Jerusalem; and there was none to bury them.
Rev 2:10

Fear none of those things which thou shalt suffer: behold, the devil shall cast some of you into prison, that ye may be tried; and ye shall have tribulation ten days: be thou faithful unto death, and I will give thee a crown of life.
corruption_summary: A Waldensian farmer who defended Rorà and would not buy his family's lives with a denial of Christ.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. Janavel's defence of Rorà was the defence of a village against soldiers sent to murder it, after the treachery of the quartering, and it stands within the lawful defence of life that Scripture permits. The psalm of Asaph describes what he saw: “Their blood have they shed like water round about Jerusalem; and there was none to bury them” (Psa 79:3).

The deeper testimony is his refusal under the threat to his wife and daughters. It is easy to admire faithfulness unto death in oneself; Janavel was asked to deny Christ to save those he loved most and would not. The principle to recover is the absolute claim of Christ, “be thou faithful unto death, and I will give thee a crown of life” (Rev 2:10), which no family affection may override.
roots_lines: Hebrew paar (H6286) — to vaunt oneself, boast; Judges 7:2.
Hebrew shaphak (H8210) — to pour out, shed; Psalm 79:3.
usage: “The people that are with thee are too many for me” (Jud 7:2) — seven men at Rorà.
“the battle is not yours, but God's” (2Ch 20:15) — the mountain ambushes.
“be thou faithful unto death” (Rev 2:10) — his answer for his wife and daughters.

pos: n. (John Whitgift, c. 1530–1604, Archbishop of Canterbury from 1583, opponent of the Puritans and sponsor of the Calvinist Lambeth Articles)
etymology: Hebrew Yochanan, the LORD is gracious; English Whitgift, a Yorkshire place-name.
biblical_def: John Whitgift was Master of Trinity College, Cambridge, when the Puritan Admonition to Parliament appeared in 1572, and his Answer to it and his long exchange with Thomas Cartwright made him the chief literary defender of the Elizabethan settlement. He argued that Scripture does not prescribe one form of church government for all times, that the church may order ceremonies and polity as seems most fit so long as nothing is done contrary to the Word, and that episcopacy is lawful and suited to a Christian commonwealth. As Archbishop of Canterbury from 1583, he required every minister to subscribe three articles: the royal supremacy, that the Prayer Book and Ordinal contained nothing contrary to the Word of God, and that the Thirty-Nine Articles were agreeable to it. Through the Court of High Commission and its oath ex officio, which required accused ministers to answer questions that might incriminate them, he suspended hundreds of Puritan clergy and broke the classical movement. Yet Whitgift was himself a Calvinist in doctrine. In 1595 he approved the Lambeth Articles, which asserted unconditional predestination and the perseverance of the saints, and he was a generous founder of almshouses and a school at Croydon. His doctrine stood on Rom 8:30, “whom he did predestinate, them he also called” (Rom 8:30).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines an archbishop as a chief bishop, and conformity as compliance with the established church.
webster_full: ARCHBISH'OP, n. A chief bishop; a church dignitary of the first class, a metropolitan bishop.
CONFORM'ITY, n. Consent; compliance with the worship of the established church.
SUBSCRIP'TION, n. Consent or attestation given by underwriting the name.
scriptures: Rom 8:30
Moreover whom he did predestinate, them he also called: and whom he called, them he also justified: and whom he justified, them he also glorified.
Let all things be done decently and in order.
Mat 15:9
But in vain they do worship me, teaching for doctrines the commandments of men.
Mat 23:8
But be not ye called Rabbi: for one is your Master, even Christ; and all ye are brethren.
corruption_summary: A Calvinist archbishop who used the High Commission to silence Calvinist ministers.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. Whitgift's position was that the church has liberty to order its government and ceremonies under the general rule of 1Co 14:40, “Let all things be done decently and in order” (1Co 14:40). The Puritans answered that a liberty to impose what Christ has not commanded becomes the error of Mat 15:9, “teaching for doctrines the commandments of men” (Mat 15:9), and that the ministers of Christ are brethren under one Master, not subjects of a prelate.

The dictionary names his method as the deeper corruption. An archbishop who held the doctrines of grace silenced hundreds of preachers who held the same doctrines, for scruples about the surplice and the Prayer Book, using an oath that forced men to accuse themselves. The principle to recover is that the government of the church exists to protect the preaching of the Word, and a church that suspends its preachers to secure uniformity has forgotten what uniformity was for.
roots_summary: Greek proorizo (G4309), to predestinate; kaleo (G2564), to call; taxis (G5010), order.
usage: “whom he did predestinate, them he also called” (Rom 8:30) — the Lambeth Articles.
“decently and in order” (1Co 14:40) — his case for the settlement.
“all ye are brethren” (Mat 23:8) — the Puritan reply.

pos: n. (Edward Johnson, 1598–1672, founder of Woburn, Massachusetts, militia captain, and author of Wonder-Working Providence of Sions Saviour in New England, 1654)
etymology: Old English Eadweard, rich guardian; English Johnson, son of John.
biblical_def: Edward Johnson was a joiner of Canterbury in Kent who came to Massachusetts Bay in 1630 with John Winthrop's fleet, returned to England, and settled permanently in New England in 1636. He was a founder of the town of Woburn in 1640, its town clerk, captain of its militia, and for many years its deputy in the General Court, and he laid out the town's lands and helped gather its church. In 1654 he published in London Wonder-Working Providence of Sions Saviour in New England, the first published history of the Massachusetts colony. Johnson wrote as a soldier of Christ. He described the Puritan migration as the mustering of an army sent by Christ to a wilderness to build churches according to His Word, recounted year by year the gathering of churches and towns, the founding of Harvard College, the trials of the Antinomian crisis and the Indian wars, and celebrated the providences of God in harvest and deliverance. His prose is rough and his verse rougher, but his book preserves the self-understanding of the first generation better than any other. He saw the colony through the psalm of the vine: “Thou hast brought a vine out of Egypt: thou hast cast out the heathen, and planted it” (Psa 80:8).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines providence as the care and superintendence which God exercises over his creatures, and militia as the body of soldiers enrolled for discipline.
webster_full: PROV'IDENCE, n. In theology, the care and superintendence which God exercises over his creatures.
MILI'TIA, n. The body of soldiers in a state enrolled for discipline, but not engaged in actual service except in emergencies.
WIL'DERNESS, n. A desert; a tract of land or region uncultivated and uninhabited by human beings.
scriptures: Psa 80:8
Thou hast brought a vine out of Egypt: thou hast cast out the heathen, and planted it.
Psa 80:9
Thou preparedst room before it, and didst cause it to take deep root, and it filled the land.
Behold, I will do a new thing; now it shall spring forth; shall ye not know it? I will even make a way in the wilderness, and rivers in the desert.
The LORD shall fight for you, and ye shall hold your peace.
corruption_summary: A Woburn captain who wrote the Puritan migration as Christ's army in the wilderness.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. Johnson's reading of New England as Israel planted in a new land is easily criticized, and the honest caveat is real: the psalm of the vine belongs to the church, not to any colony, and the identification of a Christian people with Israel driving out the nations licensed hard dealing with the natives. The vine of Psa 80 is fulfilled in Christ and His church, and its planting is spiritual.

The principle to recover from his book is its central conviction, that God works in history and His people should record His works. The prophet's promise, “I will even make a way in the wilderness, and rivers in the desert” (Isa 43:19), was the colonists' experience, and Moses' word at the sea, “The LORD shall fight for you, and ye shall hold your peace” (Exo 14:14), was their confession.
roots_summary: Hebrew gephen (H1612), vine; nata (H5193), to plant; sheresh (H8327), to take root.
usage: “Thou hast brought a vine out of Egypt” (Psa 80:8) — the Puritan migration as he saw it.
“didst cause it to take deep root” (Psa 80:9) — churches and towns gathered.
“I will even make a way in the wilderness” (Isa 43:19) — wonder-working providence.

pos: n. (the confessional Particular Baptists of the Philadelphia and Charleston associations, as distinguished from the Separate Baptists of the Southern frontier)
etymology: Latin regularis, according to rule; Greek baptistes, one who baptizes.
biblical_def: The Regular Baptists were so called in eighteenth-century America to distinguish them from the Separate Baptists who arose out of the Great Awakening. They were the older Particular Baptist churches of the middle colonies and the South, organized in the Philadelphia Association from 1707 and the Charleston Association from 1751, holding the Second London Confession in its Philadelphia form, valuing an educated ministry, and governing their churches by a settled order of discipline and association. To the Regulars, the Separates seemed disorderly: given to emotional excesses, multiplying rites, licensing women to exhort, and suspicious of confessions. To the Separates, the Regulars seemed cold and formal. But the two shared the doctrines of grace and believer's baptism, and their common persecution in Virginia and the common struggle for religious liberty drew them together. In 1787 the Regular and Separate Baptists of Virginia united as the United Baptist Churches of Christ, receiving the Philadelphia Confession while declaring that it should not be used to bind every particular, and the Kentucky Baptists followed in 1801. The union combined Regular order with Separate fervour and shaped the Baptist South. The Regulars' rule was the apostle's: “Let all things be done decently and in order” (1Co 14:40).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines regular as conformed to a rule, agreeable to an established rule, law or principle.
webster_full: REG'ULAR, a. Conformed to a rule; agreeable to an established rule, law or principle; to a prescribed mode, or to established customary forms.
UN'ION, n. The act of joining two or more things into one; concord; agreement and conjunction of mind.
OR'DER, n. Regular government; due subordination; regular disposition or methodical arrangement of things.
scriptures: Let all things be done decently and in order.
Tit 1:9
Holding fast the faithful word as he hath been taught, that he may be able by sound doctrine both to exhort and to convince the gainsayers.
Jer 6:16
Thus saith the LORD, Stand ye in the ways, and see, and ask for the old paths, where is the good way, and walk therein, and ye shall find rest for your souls. But they said, We will not walk therein.
Eph 4:3
Endeavouring to keep the unity of the Spirit in the bond of peace.
corruption_summary: The confessional Baptists of the old associations, who joined the Separates to make the United Baptists.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The name itself is an argument: the Regulars were regular because they kept a rule, the confession and discipline received from their fathers, and they asked for the old paths, “where is the good way, and walk therein” (Jer 6:16). Their temptation was formality, and the Separates reminded them that order without fire leaves churches cold.

The principle to recover is the one their union demonstrated: “Endeavouring to keep the unity of the Spirit in the bond of peace” (Eph 4:3) among believers who agree in the gospel and differ in temperament. The honest caveat is that the union's loose terms of subscription let later generations drift from the confession entirely, and a minister must still be “Holding fast the faithful word as he hath been taught” (Tit 1:9).
roots_summary: Greek taxis (G5010), order; antecho (G472), to hold fast; Hebrew nathiyb (H5410), path.
usage: “decently and in order” (1Co 14:40) — the Regular ideal.
“ask for the old paths” (Jer 6:16) — the confession received.
“the unity of the Spirit in the bond of peace” (Eph 4:3) — the union of 1787.
